name: Complete Blood Count (CBC)
measures: Counts and sizes your red cells, white cells and platelets — 21 parameters from one tube of blood.
why: It's the first test most doctors order. Low hemoglobin points to anaemia, unusual white counts to infection, low platelets to dengue or other causes.
prep: No fasting needed. Any time of day works.

faqs.q: Does a CBC need fasting?
faqs.a: No. You can eat and drink normally before a CBC.

faqs.q: What does a CBC detect?
faqs.a: Anaemia, most infections, platelet problems and several blood disorders. It flags issues; your doctor interprets them.

name: Thyroid Profile (T3, T4, TSH)
measures: TSH plus the two thyroid hormones T3 and T4.
why: Tiredness, weight change, hair fall and irregular periods often trace back to the thyroid. TSH alone misses some cases; the full profile doesn't.
prep: No fasting. Morning samples give the most consistent TSH values.

faqs.q: Should I take my thyroid tablet before the test?
faqs.a: Give your sample first, then take the tablet. Levothyroxine taken just before can push T4 up temporarily.

faqs.q: Is fasting needed for a thyroid test?
faqs.a: No, though labs prefer morning samples because TSH swings through the day.

name: HbA1c (Glycated Hemoglobin)
measures: Your average blood sugar over the last 2–3 months, as a percentage.
why: One-off sugar readings jump around. HbA1c doesn't, which is why doctors use it to diagnose diabetes and track control.
prep: No fasting needed — a key advantage over the fasting glucose test.

faqs.q: What is a normal HbA1c?
faqs.a: Below 5.7% is typical, 5.7–6.4% is prediabetes, 6.5% or above suggests diabetes. Cut-offs vary slightly by lab.

faqs.q: Can I eat before an HbA1c test?
faqs.a: Yes. Food on the day doesn't change a 3-month average.

name: Fasting Blood Sugar (FBS)
measures: Your blood glucose after an overnight fast.
why: Cheap, quick and still the standard first check for diabetes, usually paired with HbA1c.
prep: Fast 8–12 hours. Water is fine; tea and coffee are not.

faqs.q: How long should I fast?
faqs.a: 8 to 12 hours. Longer than 14 hours can skew the value the other way.

faqs.q: What counts as a normal fasting sugar?
faqs.a: 70–99 mg/dL is typical. 100–125 suggests prediabetes; 126 or above on two occasions suggests diabetes.

name: Lipid Profile
measures: Total, HDL and LDL cholesterol, triglycerides, and their ratios — 8 parameters.
why: High LDL and triglycerides quietly damage arteries for years before symptoms. This is the test that catches it early.
prep: Most labs ask for a 10–12 hour fast, though many now accept non-fasting samples. Follow what your lab says.

faqs.q: Is fasting compulsory for a lipid profile?
faqs.a: Guidelines now allow non-fasting samples for screening, but Indian labs mostly still ask for 10–12 hours. Triglycerides read higher after food.

faqs.q: How often should I check cholesterol?
faqs.a: Once a year if values are normal; every 3–6 months if you're on statins or changing diet, as your doctor advises.

name: Liver Function Test (LFT)
measures: Bilirubin, liver enzymes (SGPT, SGOT, ALP, GGT) and proteins — 11 parameters.
why: Fatty liver is common in India and shows no symptoms early. Raised enzymes are usually the first clue.
prep: Fast 8–10 hours for the cleanest readings. Skip alcohol for 24 hours before.

faqs.q: Why are SGPT and SGOT raised?
faqs.a: Common causes: fatty liver, alcohol, some medicines, and viral hepatitis. One raised reading needs a repeat, not panic.

faqs.q: Do I need to stop medicines before an LFT?
faqs.a: No — but list them for your doctor, since several common drugs nudge liver enzymes.

name: Kidney Function Test (KFT)
measures: Creatinine, urea, uric acid and electrolytes — 10 parameters covering how well your kidneys filter.
why: Diabetes and high BP damage kidneys silently. Creatinine rises only after real damage, so regular checks matter if you have either.
prep: No fasting strictly needed; many labs bundle it with fasting tests anyway.

faqs.q: What creatinine level is worrying?
faqs.a: Above roughly 1.3 mg/dL for men or 1.1 for women deserves a doctor's look — muscular builds run slightly higher naturally.

faqs.q: Does drinking less water affect the KFT?
faqs.a: Yes, dehydration can bump urea and creatinine. Drink normally before the test.

name: Vitamin D (25-OH)
measures: The storage form of vitamin D in your blood.
why: Most urban Indians test low. Deficiency shows up as body aches, low mood and weak bones, and it's cheap to fix once confirmed.
prep: No fasting needed.

faqs.q: What level of vitamin D is low?
faqs.a: Below 20 ng/mL is deficient, 20–30 insufficient, 30–100 adequate. Supplements are dosed to the number, so test before you dose.

faqs.q: Why is the vitamin D test costlier than others?
faqs.a: It runs on immunoassay analysers with pricier reagents. Package bundles usually price it better than standalone.

name: Vitamin B12
measures: The B12 level in your blood.
why: Vegetarian diets often run low. Deficiency causes fatigue, tingling in hands and feet, and memory fog — all reversible if caught.
prep: An 8-hour fast is usually advised. Skip B12 supplements for a few days before, or the result reads falsely high.

faqs.q: What is a normal B12 level?
faqs.a: Roughly 200–900 pg/mL. Symptoms can appear even in the low-normal range, so discuss borderline values.

faqs.q: Should I stop my multivitamin before testing B12?
faqs.a: Yes, for 3–4 days if your doctor agrees — supplements inflate the reading.

name: Urine Routine & Microscopy
measures: Physical, chemical and microscopic examination of urine — protein, sugar, infection markers and more.
why: A ₹100-odd test that catches urine infections, early kidney trouble and uncontrolled diabetes.
prep: First morning sample is best. Collect mid-stream in the sterile container the lab gives you.

faqs.q: How do I collect a mid-stream sample?
faqs.a: Start passing urine, then collect from the middle of the stream. The first flush carries skin bacteria that spoil results.

faqs.q: Protein in urine — serious?
faqs.a: Trace protein after fever or exercise is common. Persistent protein needs kidney follow-up.

name: ESR (Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate)
measures: How fast your red cells settle in an hour — a rough marker of inflammation.
why: Old but useful: persistently high ESR supports diagnoses like TB, arthritis and chronic infection.
prep: No fasting needed.

faqs.q: What raises ESR?
faqs.a: Any inflammation — infection, autoimmune disease, even pregnancy and age. It says something is on; it doesn't say what.

faqs.q: ESR vs CRP — which is better?
faqs.a: CRP moves faster with acute infection; ESR suits slow, chronic conditions. Doctors often order both.

name: CRP (C-Reactive Protein)
measures: A protein your liver releases within hours of inflammation starting.
why: Rises fast in bacterial infection and falls fast with treatment, so doctors use it to judge whether antibiotics are working.
prep: No fasting needed.

faqs.q: What CRP level indicates infection?
faqs.a: Above 10 mg/L usually means active inflammation; very high values lean bacterial. Trends matter more than one number.

faqs.q: Is CRP the same as hs-CRP?
faqs.a: No. hs-CRP measures tiny elevations for heart-risk scoring; regular CRP tracks infection and inflammation.

name: Uric Acid
measures: The uric acid level in your blood.
why: High levels crystallise in joints as gout — classically a hot, swollen big toe — and can form kidney stones.
prep: No fasting strictly needed; avoid a heavy non-veg meal the night before.

faqs.q: What foods raise uric acid?
faqs.a: Red meat, organ meat, seafood, beer and sugary drinks. Dal in normal amounts is fine for most people despite the myth.

faqs.q: High uric acid but no pain — treat it?
faqs.a: Often just diet and rechecks. Medicines usually start only after gout attacks or stones. Your doctor decides.

name: Iron Studies
measures: Serum iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation and ferritin — the full picture of iron stores.
why: Anaemia treatment differs by cause. These four values tell iron-deficiency apart from other anaemias so you don't take iron blindly.
prep: Morning fasting sample; skip iron tablets that morning.

faqs.q: Why test ferritin along with iron?
faqs.a: Serum iron swings daily; ferritin reflects stored iron. Low ferritin is the surest sign of iron deficiency.

faqs.q: Can I take my iron tablet before the test?
faqs.a: No — take it after the sample, or the reading shoots up misleadingly.

name: Ferritin
measures: Your body's stored iron.
why: The single best test for iron deficiency — it falls before hemoglobin does. Also checked in hair fall and restless legs.
prep: No fasting needed.

faqs.q: What is a normal ferritin level?
faqs.a: Roughly 20–250 ng/mL for men, 10–120 for women; lab ranges vary. Hair-fall clinics often aim above 50.

faqs.q: Can ferritin be high without excess iron?
faqs.a: Yes — it also rises with inflammation and fatty liver, so doctors read it alongside CRP.

name: Serum Electrolytes
measures: Sodium, potassium and chloride.
why: Checked in weakness, vomiting, dehydration and for anyone on BP medicines or diuretics, which quietly shift these values.
prep: No fasting needed.

faqs.q: Why did my doctor order electrolytes with my BP medicine?
faqs.a: Several BP drugs move potassium up or down. A yearly check catches it before it causes trouble.

faqs.q: What are symptoms of low sodium?
faqs.a: Nausea, headache, confusion and fatigue — common in older adults and often found only on testing.

name: Serum Calcium
measures: The calcium level in your blood.
why: Ordered for bone pain, kidney stones and thyroid/parathyroid issues. Usually read together with vitamin D and albumin.
prep: No fasting needed; skip calcium supplements that morning.

faqs.q: Does low blood calcium mean weak bones?
faqs.a: Not directly — blood calcium stays stable by drawing from bone. Bone strength needs a DEXA scan; this test screens for other disorders.

faqs.q: What causes high calcium?
faqs.a: Most often parathyroid overactivity or vitamin D excess. Persistent high values always deserve follow-up.

name: Testosterone (Total)
measures: Total testosterone in blood.
why: Checked for low energy, low libido and fertility work-ups in men, and PCOS work-ups in women.
prep: Sample before 10 am — levels drop through the day. No fasting needed.

faqs.q: Why must testosterone be tested in the morning?
faqs.a: Levels peak early morning and fall 20–30% by evening. Morning sampling keeps results comparable.

faqs.q: One low testosterone report — do I need treatment?
faqs.a: No. Guidelines ask for at least two morning samples plus symptoms before any therapy talk.

name: Prolactin
measures: The prolactin hormone level.
why: Part of irregular-period, infertility and milky-discharge work-ups; also checked with some psychiatric medicines.
prep: Sample 3–4 hours after waking, rested. Stress and even a difficult blood draw can raise it.

faqs.q: Why was I asked to sit calmly before the prolactin test?
faqs.a: Prolactin rises with stress, exercise and stimulation. Ten quiet minutes before the draw avoids a false high.

faqs.q: Mildly high prolactin — what next?
faqs.a: Usually a repeat under proper conditions first. Persistent high values get a medicine review and sometimes imaging.

name: PSA (Prostate-Specific Antigen)
measures: A protein made by the prostate.
why: The standard screen for prostate enlargement and cancer risk in men over 50, or earlier with family history.
prep: No fasting. Avoid cycling, ejaculation and prostate exams for 48 hours before — each can raise PSA.

faqs.q: What is a normal PSA?
faqs.a: Under 4 ng/mL is the usual cut-off, but age-specific ranges apply and trends matter more than one value.

faqs.q: Does high PSA mean cancer?
faqs.a: Not by itself — infection, enlargement and recent activity all raise it. It flags who needs a urologist's assessment.

name: HIV Screening (1 & 2)
measures: Antibodies to HIV-1 and HIV-2 (and the p24 antigen in duo tests).
why: Standard before surgeries and in pregnancy, and the only way to know status after possible exposure. Reports are confidential.
prep: No fasting. Remember the window period: test 3–4 weeks after exposure for duo tests, with a confirmatory repeat later.

faqs.q: How soon after exposure can HIV be detected?
faqs.a: 4th-generation duo tests detect most infections by 3–4 weeks. A negative before 3 months usually gets one repeat to confirm.

faqs.q: Is my HIV report kept private?
faqs.a: Yes. Indian law and lab policy both require confidentiality, and reputable labs share results only with you.

name: HBsAg (Hepatitis B Surface Antigen)
measures: The surface protein of the hepatitis B virus.
why: Hepatitis B often shows no symptoms for years while it damages the liver. Standard before surgery, in pregnancy and for household contacts of carriers.
prep: No fasting needed.

faqs.q: HBsAg positive — what does it mean?
faqs.a: Current infection, recent or chronic. Follow-up tests sort out which, and many chronic carriers just need monitoring.

faqs.q: I'm vaccinated — will HBsAg show positive?
faqs.a: No. Vaccination produces antibodies, not the antigen this test looks for.

name: Beta hCG (Pregnancy Hormone)
measures: The exact level of the pregnancy hormone hCG in blood.
why: Detects pregnancy days earlier than urine kits and, tracked over 48 hours, tells doctors whether an early pregnancy is progressing normally.
prep: No fasting, any time of day.

faqs.q: How early can beta hCG detect pregnancy?
faqs.a: About 8–10 days after conception — several days before a home urine kit turns positive.

faqs.q: Why repeat beta hCG after 48 hours?
faqs.a: In early pregnancy the value should roughly double every two days. The trend matters more than the single number.

name: D-Dimer
measures: A fragment released when blood clots break down.
why: Ordered urgently for suspected leg-vein clots or lung clots. A normal value largely rules them out; a high one triggers scans.
prep: No fasting. Usually ordered same-day by a doctor rather than as a routine screen.

faqs.q: What does a high D-Dimer mean?
faqs.a: Possible clot — but also infection, surgery, pregnancy or age. It rules out clots well; it doesn't confirm them.

faqs.q: Should I get a D-Dimer as a routine checkup?
faqs.a: No. It's a targeted test for suspected clotting, best ordered by a doctor with a reason.

name: Dengue NS1 Antigen
measures: A dengue virus protein detectable from day 1 of fever.
why: In monsoon season, this is the earliest reliable dengue test — positive before antibodies appear. Usually paired with a CBC to watch platelets.
prep: No fasting. Best within the first 5 days of fever.

faqs.q: When should I test NS1 after fever starts?
faqs.a: Day 1 to day 5 of fever. After day 5 it fades and the IgM antibody test takes over.

faqs.q: NS1 positive — is hospital admission needed?
faqs.a: Most dengue is managed at home with fluids and daily platelet monitoring. Warning signs like bleeding or severe pain need hospital review.
